20: 
21: A chatbot writes the first piece of its answer, reads everything again including that piece, and writes the next. Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown puts it plainly: the model assigns "a probability to all possible next words", and then one is picked [@3b1b-llm-briefly]. Stephen Wolfram describes ChatGPT as "just asking over and over again" what the next word should be [@wolfram-chatgpt].

31: {{figure next-word-machine-pick | One step of the loop. The model scores every candidate for the next token, picks one, appends it, and runs again on the longer text. A 300-word answer is a few hundred of these steps. | Illustrative probabilities}}
32: 
33: Step 3 says "a likely" piece on purpose. Products sample, so a less likely token sometimes wins. A setting called [[temperature]] controls how often. Wolfram reports that for essays a temperature of 0.8 "seems best", a value found by trying things out; no theory produced it [@wolfram-chatgpt]. Chat products also go through a second round of training on example conversations and human ratings, which is what turns a raw text-continuer into something that answers questions politely. The loop underneath stays the same.

Every answer is a fresh draw from the same probabilities. 29: ::: principle The physics of interaction cost
30: 1. Human cognitive processing operates on rigid neurological thresholds: 100 milliseconds feels instantaneous, 1,000 milliseconds preserves uninterrupted thought continuity, and 10 seconds marks the limit of focused attention [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci].
31: 2. Total interaction cost is the additive sum of physical motor effort (keystrokes, pointer traversal) and cognitive effort (prompt formulation, working memory retention, output parsing).
32: 3. Conversational chat interfaces impose maximum interaction cost: the user must context-switch, type complex natural language queries, and parse conversational prose to extract structured facts.

37: ## Perceptual physics and the 1.2-second glance rule
38: 
39: To design effective [[agentic-ux|agentic UX]], product teams must ground interface timing in the empirical perceptual physics established by Stuart Card, Thomas Moran, and Allen Newell at Xerox PARC [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci]:
40: 
41: - **100 Milliseconds (Perceptual Causality):** When a visual surface updates within 100ms of user input, the human brain registers the change as an immediate physical consequence of motor action. This is the realm of direct manipulation: moving a canvas card, resizing a column, or pressing a button.

88: ::: stat 12% vs 78% 89: In enterprise workflow applications, transitioning from a reactive sidebar chatbot to an inline ambient HUD lifted weekly active adoption from 12% to 78% while cutting median task completion time from 118 seconds to 4.2 seconds. 90: Sources: [@cagan-transformed-ai] [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci] 91: ::: 92:

206: ::: answers
207: 1. The three thresholds are 100ms (perceived as immediate, direct physical causality), 1,000ms (the boundary of uninterrupted human thought continuity), and 10,000ms (the limit of focused attention before task abandonment) [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci]. Conversational chat violates the 1,000ms threshold because typing a multi-sentence prompt, awaiting network and model generation, and parsing conversational text takes 15 to 60 seconds, completely shattering working memory and thought continuity.
208: 2. Redesign: When a customer calls, an ambient HUD analyzes the account record and automatically displays an inline recommendation banner: *"Eligible for ₹500 goodwill refund due to 45-minute delivery delay."* The representative reviews the recommendation and clicks a single *"Approve Refund"* button (0 keystrokes, 1 click, 3 seconds). Time saved: $(90\text{s} - 3\text{s}) \times 10{,}000 = 870{,}000\text{ seconds} \approx \mathbf{241.7\text{ hours monthly}}$, eliminating user fatigue and accelerating call resolution.
209: 3. When an automated agent achieves high reliability ($\ge 95\%$), human vigilance naturally decays (Bainbridge's ironies of automation); operators assume the system is correct and begin rubber-stamping approvals without reading. Two safeguards: (a) Cognitive speed-bumps on high-risk actions, requiring the user to inspect a highlighted diff or select an explicit confirmation rationale, and (b) Visual diff emphasis (red strikethrough deletions and green insertions) paired with periodic blind audit samples that test whether operators notice deliberate test discrepancies.

14: ---
15: 
16: A user types an inquiry into a modern financial search bar: *"Compare capital gains tax liability on equity versus debt mutual funds held for two years under the latest Indian Finance Act."* The interface locks. The submit button freezes. For 4.2 seconds, the screen presents a blank canvas before a generic loading spinner appears. At 7.8 seconds, a dense 400-word paragraph abruptly pops into the viewport. Although the tax calculation is mathematically sound, the customer experiences the interface as broken, sluggish, and unresponsive. Human interaction with software is bounded by biological constants. In their foundational cognitive architecture research, Stuart Card, Thomas Moran, and Allen Newell established that human perception operates on rigid neurological thresholds: 100 milliseconds feels instantaneous, 1,000 milliseconds preserves the unbroken train of thought, and 10 seconds marks the absolute boundary of user attention [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci]. When software violates those biological limits, cognitive engagement collapses. ==In generative product engineering, latency is not a technical afterthought—it is the primary determinant of cognitive engagement, user trust, and commercial retention.==
17: 
18: ## Deconstructing the latency equation

50: 
51: ::: principle The latency budget hierarchy
52: 1. Human cognitive perception is bounded by biological constants: 100 milliseconds is perceived as immediate direct manipulation, 1,000 milliseconds maintains fluid thought continuity, and 10 seconds represents the maximum tolerance for task completion [@card-moran-newell-psychology-hci].
53: 2. Generative language models do not compute completions in a single instantaneous step; they process inputs through a prompt prefill phase followed by sequential autoregressive token generation.
54: 3. Total end-to-end response time is the additive sum of network transit, server queue latency, Time-to-First-Token ($TTFT$), and token generation duration ($N_{\text{output}} / TPS$).
